title: Codeine-Induced Constipation - Young Woman with Lower Abdominal Pain
patient_instructions: You are Chloe Bennett, a 20-year-old woman with a week of dull, moderate (4/10) pain across your whole lower tummy that seems a bit worse after eating, with no particular food trigger. A week ago you hurt your lower back; a doctor said it was 'just regular back pain' and gave you Panadeine Forte (paracetamol and codeine), which you have been taking regularly. Your back is now much better. If asked directly about bowels: you have not opened your bowels properly for about 5 days, your stools are hard, you strain, but you are still passing wind and you have NOT been vomiting. Your periods are normal, no vaginal bleeding or discharge, last period 2 weeks ago; you are not pregnant as far as you know. Only reveal the codeine when the candidate asks what treatment you took for the back pain. Ideas: you think the pain is 'something I ate'. Concerns: you are worried something is seriously wrong in your tummy. Expectations: you want the pain sorted. Affect: mildly uncomfortable, cooperative, a little embarrassed discussing bowels.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor at a rural NSW practice. Chloe Bennett, a 20-year-old woman, presents with a week of lower abdominal pain. Tasks: (1) Take a focused, structured history for approximately 4 minutes, including a bowel-habit and medication history. (2) State the physical examination findings you would seek from the examiner. (3) Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient in plain language.
examiner_instructions: The diagnosis lies in the medication history: regular codeine (Panadeine Forte) causing opioid-induced constipation. Reward candidates who take a full medication history exploring the recent back-pain treatment, and who ask a proper bowel-habit set (last motion, frequency, consistency/Bristol, straining, passing wind, vomiting) to separate simple constipation from impaction and obstruction. On examination the expected findings are palpable faecal loading in the left lower quadrant and hard faeces on DRE, with NEGATIVE peritonism (no rigidity, guarding or rebound) and a NEGATIVE pregnancy test. Note for the examiner: if peritonism or a positive pregnancy test were genuinely present, the correct action is urgent surgical/senior review or exclusion of ectopic pregnancy, not reassurance. Prompt if needed: 'What did she take for the back pain?'

criteria: Confirms haemodynamic stability and takes a systematic pain assessment
Takes a full medication history eliciting regular codeine (Panadeine Forte)
Asks a structured bowel-habit set (last motion, consistency, straining, passing wind, vomiting)
Screens GI, KUB and pelvic groups and excludes obstruction features
Uses passing wind and absence of vomiting to reason against bowel obstruction
Recognises the obstruction variant (absolute constipation + vomiting + distension) as the key differential
Cease/wean codeine and substitute non-opioid analgesia for the back pain
First-line laxatives per eTG (osmotic e.g. macrogol +/- stimulant e.g. senna), fluids, fibre, activity
Safety-nets for obstruction (review if no bowel motion in 48-72h or vomiting/distension develops)
Sensitive, plain-language explanation linking the painkiller to the constipation
Checks understanding and counsels on prophylactic laxatives with any opioid

red_flags: Absolute constipation (no faeces or flatus) + vomiting + distension/colicky pain indicates bowel obstruction - ED referral, nil by mouth, IV fluids, imaging
Peritonism (rigidity, guarding, rebound) is incompatible with simple constipation and mandates urgent surgical review
A positive pregnancy test in a young woman with abdominal pain requires exclusion of ectopic pregnancy and changes the whole approach
Opioid-induced constipation does not develop tolerance - ongoing opioids need prophylactic laxatives
australian_guidelines: eTG: first-line laxative therapy for constipation - an osmotic laxative (e.g. macrogol) +/- a stimulant (e.g. senna), with fluid, fibre and activity advice
TGA up-scheduling (from 1 February 2018): all codeine-containing analgesics are prescription-only (Schedule 4); eTG/RACGP discourage codeine for uncomplicated low back pain
eTG / RACGP: prescribe prophylactic laxatives whenever an opioid is continued, because opioid-induced constipation does not develop tolerance
Substitute non-opioid analgesia (paracetamol +/- NSAID) for resolved musculoskeletal back pain; call 000 / ED referral if obstruction develops
learning_objectives: Recognise that the diagnosis can sit in the medication history rather than the pain history
Take a structured bowel-habit history to distinguish constipation, impaction and obstruction
Apply Australian laxative and opioid-prescribing guidance
Counsel on prophylactic laxatives with opioid analgesia
key_points: Panadeine Forte is paracetamol 500 mg + codeine 30 mg; codeine reliably causes constipation
Palpable faecal loading in the LLQ and hard faeces on DRE with no peritonism support simple constipation
Passing wind and no vomiting argue against obstruction; the reverse should trigger ED referral
Always take a medication history - the diagnosis is a drug side effect

citations.claim: Constipation assessment, masquerades, alternation with diarrhoea, and disimpaction/referral thresholds are covered in Murtagh's constipation chapter, against which this diagnosis and impaction/obstruction differential are consistent.
Australian laxative options for constipation management support first-line laxative therapy after ceasing codeine.
Drugs as a cause of a puzzling presentation ('Drugs - is the patient trying to tell me something?') underpins always taking a medication history, because the diagnosis sits in the drug history.
